slides.title: AI Smart-Building Log Analysis
slides.subtitle: Reproducible anomaly detection for CU-BEMS data
slides.kicker: Project Proposal | Smart Facilities SA | Group C262T-4201 D01
slides.speaker_notes: Good morning. Our project is called AI Smart-Building Log Analysis. In this presentation, I will explain the problem, the dataset, our planned pipeline, the anomaly-detection methods, and how we will evaluate the prototype. The main idea is simple: we want to turn complex building logs into useful evidence for human review.

slides.title: Why AI is useful here
slides.subtitle: Frequent logs create a review burden.

cards.title: Operational scale
cards.body: Frequent signals across floors and systems.

cards.title: Context matters
cards.body: Normal behaviour changes by time and location.

cards.title: Decision support
cards.body: Alerts need evidence for human review.

slides.takeaway: The project supports investigation; it does not automate control.
slides.speaker_notes: The motivation is that smart buildings produce many signals. These signals can show energy use, indoor temperature, humidity and lighting conditions. However, normal behaviour is not the same everywhere in a building. A fixed rule may miss important patterns, and manual checking is not realistic. So our goal is decision support. We want to highlight unusual behaviour, but we do not want the system to make automatic operational decisions.

slides.title: CU-BEMS defines the research boundary
slides.subtitle: Representative data, not a live deployment.

cards.title: 7 floors
cards.body: Minute-level records from a multi-floor academic office building.

cards.title: 18 months
cards.body: The selected record spans July 2018 to December 2019.

cards.title: 6 signal groups
cards.body: AC, lighting, plug load, temperature, humidity and illuminance.

slides.takeaway: The dataset supports prototype research, but not every live-building scenario.
slides.speaker_notes: For the project, we will use the CU-BEMS Energy Research Data from the Chamchuri 5 building. It includes minute-level measurements from seven floors over about eighteen months. The signals include three power-system groups and three indoor-environment groups. This gives us a reproducible dataset. But there is also a limit: it does not represent every Smart Facilities SA system, and it does not include confirmed incident labels.

slides.title: Scope stays analytical
slides.subtitle: Prototype first, production later.
slides.verdict: This keeps the project feasible within ten teaching weeks.
slides.speaker_notes: The project scope is important. We are not building a production monitoring platform, and we are not controlling physical equipment. We are also not installing new sensors or confirming every detected anomaly as a real incident. Instead, the project focuses on data preparation, feature engineering, anomaly analysis, visualisation and prioritisation. This makes the work achievable within the ten-week timeframe.

slides.title: A reproducible pipeline links data to evidence
slides.subtitle: Five stages with audit trails.

chart.title: Pipeline stages
chart.notes: Import, clean, feature, detect and explain.

slides.message: The pipeline is a research artifact, not only code.
slides.speaker_notes: Our pipeline has five main stages. First, we import the CU-BEMS data and keep the raw data unchanged. Second, we clean and integrate the files into a consistent structure. Third, we create features, such as rolling statistics and time-based patterns. Fourth, we run anomaly-detection methods. Finally, we explain the results with visualisations. This structure is important because a reviewer should be able to understand how each result was produced.

slides.title: Methods compare clarity with pattern sensitivity
slides.subtitle: Advanced does not automatically mean better.

table.caption: Candidate examples include z-scores, rolling deviations, Isolation Forest and LOF.

slides.takeaway: The chosen method should be stable, useful and explainable.
slides.speaker_notes: We will compare two method families. The first family is interpretable statistical baselines, such as thresholds, z-scores, robust scores and rolling deviations. These are easy to explain and give us a clear benchmark. The second family is unsupervised machine learning, such as Isolation Forest and Local Outlier Factor. These methods may detect more complex patterns, but they must be tuned carefully. We will compare usefulness, stability and interpretability.

slides.title: Evaluation fits unlabeled anomaly data
slides.subtitle: Alerts are candidates, not confirmed faults.

quadrants.title: Stability checks
quadrants.body: Compare time, floor and zone subsets.

slides.summary_callout: The evaluation asks whether alerts are consistent, explainable and reviewable.
slides.speaker_notes: A key challenge is that the dataset does not have trustworthy labels for true faults. So we cannot rely on normal classification metrics as the main measure. Instead, we will use a multi-part evaluation. We will inject controlled synthetic anomalies, test stability across data subsets, check alert volume, and review representative cases. This is more honest for this project, because an anomaly is not automatically a real equipment failure.

slides.title: The highest risks are knowable early
slides.subtitle: Audit first, then model.

chart.title: Risk probability scores
chart.notes: Early mitigation: data audit, baseline models and explicit uncertainty.

slides.message: The main mitigation is earlier evidence and clearer limits.
slides.speaker_notes: This slide shows the main risks from the proposal. The highest risk is the lack of trustworthy anomaly labels. The next major risk is data quality, including missing or noisy measurements. Integration across floors, zones and measurement types is also important. Our mitigation strategy is to do the data audit early, start with interpretable baselines, compare methods, and clearly document uncertainty.

slides.title: Deliverables turn the prototype into evidence
slides.subtitle: Outputs are grouped for assessment.

cards.title: Build artifacts
cards.body: D1 pipeline, D2 patterns and D3 model comparison.

cards.title: Interpretation artifacts
cards.body: D4 visualisation and D5 prioritisation framework.

cards.title: Handover artifacts
cards.body: D6 technical report and D7 reproducible package.

slides.takeaway: Success depends on reproducibility, validity and interpretability.
slides.speaker_notes: The proposal defines seven deliverables. The first group is build artifacts: the data-preparation pipeline, pattern analysis and model comparison. The second group is interpretation artifacts: visualisation and anomaly prioritisation. The final group is handover artifacts: the final technical report and reproducible package. The important point is that success is not only about producing a model. It is also about producing evidence that another technical reviewer can understand and reproduce.

slides.title: The 10-week plan reduces uncertainty
slides.subtitle: Data confidence comes before handover.

chart.title: Approximate phase duration across the ten-week schedule
chart.notes: The schedule assumes the CU-BEMS dataset remains suitable after the early audit.

slides.message: By Week 10, the team should explain what the prototype detects, how reliable it is, and where it should not be overused.
slides.speaker_notes: The project runs over ten teaching weeks. The first two weeks focus on requirements and data confidence. Weeks two to four focus on preparation and pattern discovery. Weeks four to six focus on anomaly detection. Weeks six to eight focus on evaluation and visualisation. The last two weeks are for prototype review, documentation and handover. Our closing message is that the project should provide a useful and reproducible prototype, while clearly explaining its limits.
